note: IAM actions, per service, so the restriction screen offers a list instead of asking somebody to
type an action name. An action typed from memory is either wrong (and the server refuses it,
which is fine but slow) or subtly wrong in a way that still validates - sqs:DeleteMessages does
not exist, sqs:ReceiveMessages does not exist, and neither mistake is obvious on the screen.
THIS IS AN INPUT AID AND NOT A TRUST BOUNDARY. Nothing downstream believes it. The server checks
every chosen action against the actions the plan actually grants and against the protected set,
and the inline writer checks them again against the fence it is handed. An action absent from
this file can still be typed; an action wrongly present here is refused by those checks.
So an incomplete file costs convenience, never correctness - which is why it starts with one
service rather than waiting to be complete.
PROVENANCE: written from knowledge, not generated from the AWS Service Authorization Reference.
The reference is the authority and it is machine readable; regenerating this file from it is the
right way to add services. Until then, treat any single entry as capable of being wrong and rely
on the checks named above rather than on this list.
